why: The old copy makes good sense. The SEAL editors explain the late copy's verb "made" as a misreading of the signs of "carried," and note that the late scribe added "the gods" and swapped the general word "work" for the picture of a yoke.

p: The Assyrian copy has "those of the deep" where the old copy has "those of heaven."

why: Two copies, the oldest and a late one, agree on "heaven." The SEAL editors note that the Assyrian copy replaced it with "the deep water." The line is too broken to say more.

p: The old copy reads forty years; the Middle Babylonian copy fifty.

why: The Plain follows the oldest copy. The SEAL editors read 40 in A, as Lambert and Millard did, and reject von Soden's reading of a much larger number there.

p: The old copy says "let us confront" the throne-bearer; later copies say "let us kill him."

why: The Plain follows the oldest copy. The later copies make the rebels' plan more violent. The Middle Babylonian copy's verb is damaged; the SEAL editors think its scribe mixed the two readings.

t: Throw off the work, or break the yoke?
p: Later copies say "let us break the yoke" instead of asking the throne-bearer to lift the work.

readings.plain: and he has made our heavy work harder.

why: Where the oldest copy is broken, the Plain follows the copy that keeps the line. The SEAL editors read the verb as dunnunu, "to make strong, harder," a well-known phrase with "work."

p: The old copy writes Enlil here by mistake; the sense needs Enki.

readings.w: SEAL's reading of A, the Old Babylonian copy written by Ipiq-Aya at Sippar under King Ammi-saduqa (British Museum, BM 78941+78943), corrected
A, the Old Babylonian copy written by Ipiq-Aya at Sippar under King Ammi-saduqa (British Museum, BM 78941+78943), as written

why: Enlil is the one speaking to, so he cannot be brought to himself, and the next lines say they brought Enki (2:64). The SEAL editors mark the sign as a scribe's slip for Enki.

p: The old copies make Enlil send Nusku; the late copies make Anu speak.

readings.w: A, the Old Babylonian copy written by Ipiq-Aya at Sippar under King Ammi-saduqa (British Museum, BM 78941+78943); F, a copy of unknown origin (BM 17596a); L, a Neo-Assyrian copy

why: The Plain follows the oldest copy. Since Anu proposed sending Nusku (2:86), the later copies give Anu the order as well; in the old copy Enlil, whose minister Nusku is, sends him.

why: The oldest copy keeps the first signs of the verb "rebel" (ibb[alkitū]), which agrees with the late Sippar copy. Most other copies end the line with "shouted."
b: Ḫupšu names commoners of low rank, men called up for work or as foot soldiers. The Igigi speak of themselves as a labor gang.

p: The Old Babylonian copy has Enki (written Ea) answer; the later copies have Anu.

why: The SEAL editors note that in the old version Ea steps in here and begins the making of humans, while in the later version the talk simply goes on with Anu's answer. The Plain follows the old copy; on the names Enki and Ea, see 1:16.

a: Doing this is not fitting for me alone.

readings.en: with me let the making be
readings.plain: Let the making be done by me.

why: The old copy fits the next lines, where Mami says the task belongs with Enki. The SEAL editors think the late scribe misread or misheard la, "not," as lu, "let it be," and then dropped a word, producing a new sentence.
